newsitem.title: UK: ICCO seen uniting on use of buffer stock sales.
newsitem.headline: ICCO seen uniting on use of buffer stock sales.

text.p: Cocoa producers and consumers at London talks neared agreement on setting up a special reserve fund with the proceeds of buffer stock sales, delegates said on Thursday.

The delegates to a three-day International Cocoa Organization (ICCO) meeting said on Thursday producers and consumers were likely to unite for a fund of three million stg, but were likely to defer a decision until March.
"Three million (stg) seems to be the common number," said Tim Mordan, the UK delegate and chairman of the ICCO executive committee.
Producer countries threw their weight behind a fund of between 3-4.3 milion stg, edging closer to producers' ideas of a maximum of three million.
They were previously backing the ICCO executive director Eduard Kouame who favours a larger fund of 5-6 million stg to generate more interest income for the group's activities.

The sticking point was how to allocate a last tranche of some $330 million expected to pile up in ICCO coffers from the sale of 250,000 tonnes of buffer stock cocoa by 1998. These were gathered through a levy system mostly charged on producers. The delegates agreed in principle to set-aside some $4 million surplus profit expected from the sale of buffer stocks. This is based on the average price of cocoa sold which has so far exceeded by $37 the targeted $1,300 a tonne. "Everything depends on the level of (buffer stock) profits. We will pray that we have profits," said Antoine A Delon, the London representative of the Ivory Coast commodities sector.

The fund will be kept as reserve for a future liquidation of the organization but the ICCO plans to use the interest income to cover costs when buffer stocks dry up in 1998. These have financed some 40 percent of the ICCO budget in the past years.
